titre: The Modesty That Invented the Stethoscope
accroche: In 1816, a doctor too embarrassed to press his ear to a patient's chest rolls up a sheet of paper, and invents an instrument
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1816, at the Hôpital Necker, René Laennec examines a young, heavyset patient whom he suspects of having heart disease. His master Jean-Nicolas Corvisart has taught him percussion: placing the fingers on the chest and tapping to deduce the state of the organs. Laennec also combines it with direct auscultation, the ear pressed against the patient's chest, a gesture his master did not teach him but which Laennec practices on his own. With this patient, percussion proves inconclusive because of her corpulence, and pressing his ear against her chest seems improper given her age and sex.

## A Childhood Memory

He then remembers a scene observed in the Louvre garden: one child scratches the end of a long piece of wood with a pin, while another listens at the other end and perceives the amplified sound. Laennec rolls a sheet of paper into a cylinder, places one end on his patient's chest, presses his ear to the other end, and hears the heartbeats with a clarity he had never achieved with the bare ear.

He does not stop at this improvisation. He tests several materials, paper, wood, the Indian cane, and settles on a wooden cylinder twenty-five centimeters long, fitted with a removable conical mouthpiece, in two parts that unscrew for ease of transport. He names the instrument the stethoscope, from the Greek *stethos*, the chest, and *skopein*, to examine.

## An Instrument That Becomes a Method

Laennec does not content himself with hearing better: he undertakes a systematic work of description, correlating, across hundreds of patients and then at the autopsies that follow their deaths, each sound heard with the lesion that produces it. He forges a vocabulary still in use today, rale, egophony, to designate sounds that no physician had until then had a word to distinguish. His treatise, *De l'auscultation médiate* (*On Mediate Auscultation*), published in 1819, brings together this classification.

## The Shift

The gesture Laennec sought to avoid out of modesty produced a shift wider than its initial motive: by placing an instrument between the patient's body and the doctor's ear, he moved medicine a step toward objectified examination, where diagnosis rests on a reproducible physical sign rather than on the patient's account alone. This same shift, an obstacle bypassed by a material detour, will become a way of practicing medicine well beyond auscultation. Laennec dies in 1826, at forty-five, of the tuberculosis he had spent his career listening for in others.

repere.texte: The stethoscope Laennec describes in his 1819 treatise is a wooden cylinder twenty-five centimeters long and 3.5 centimeters in diameter, fitted with a removable conical mouthpiece; it unscrews in two parts to be carried more easily.
repere.source: Farhat Yaqub, “René Théophile Hyacinthe Laënnec,” The Lancet Respiratory Medicine, 2015

carte.punch: Too embarrassed to press his ear to a patient, a doctor invents the stethoscope.
carte.idee: In 1816, René Laennec declines to examine a young patient with the bare ear. He rolls a sheet of paper into a cylinder and discovers that it transmits heart sounds with unprecedented clarity. The instrument he develops from it, described in 1819, founds modern auscultation.

quiz.question: Why does Laennec choose a cylinder rather than continuing to listen directly against the skin?
choix: Because percussion fails owing to her corpulence, and direct auscultation would be improper given her age and sex
Because a Hôpital Necker regulation forbade any physical contact between doctor and female patient
Because Corvisart had taught him direct ear auscultation, and he was only seeking to amplify it
Because he had already developed this cylinder for an acoustics experiment unrelated to medicine
quiz.explication: Laennec had learned percussion from Corvisart, but also combined it with direct ear auscultation, a gesture his master did not teach him. With this patient, percussion fails because of her corpulence, and pressing his ear against her chest seems improper given her age and sex. No hospital regulation, no prohibition from Corvisart, and no preexisting instrument explains his choice: it is a one-off improvisation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the idea for the cylinder Laennec uses to listen to his patient come from?
choix: From an instrument already used by military doctors to listen to the wounded
From a childhood memory, a scene seen in the Louvre garden
From reading an acoustics treatise published by a German physicist
From advice given by his master Corvisart, who already used this procedure
quiz_supplementaire.explication: He remembers a scene observed in the Louvre garden: one child scratches the end of a long piece of wood with a pin, while another listens at the other end and perceives the amplified sound.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What material and shape does Laennec finally settle on for his instrument, after testing several options?
choix: A rolled paper tube, reinforced with strips of leather
An Indian cane cut from a single piece, with no removable mouthpiece
A wooden cylinder twenty-five centimeters long, in two parts that unscrew
A hollow metal cylinder, lighter than wood
quiz_supplementaire.explication: After testing paper, wood, and the Indian cane, Laennec settles on a wooden cylinder twenty-five centimeters long, fitted with a removable conical mouthpiece, in two parts that unscrew for ease of transport.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the word “stethoscope” that Laennec chooses for his instrument come from?
choix: From the Latin stetho, to listen, and scopus, goal
From the name of the town where he grew up, Saint-Étienne
From a word invented by Corvisart to designate percussion
From the Greek stethos, the chest, and skopein, to examine
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Laennec names his instrument the stethoscope, from the Greek stethos, the chest, and skopein, to examine.
